title: Toronto's Largest Diwali Festival Lights Up Nathan Phillips Square
excerpt: More than 850 performers, a Diwali marketplace and a fireworks finale over City Hall anchored the free two-day Festival of Lights on October 24-25.
body:
• The Diwali Festival of Lights took over Nathan Phillips Square in downtown Toronto on October 24-25, billed by organizers and listings as Canada's largest Diwali celebration.
  • More than 850 artists performed across the two days, alongside food vendors, a Diwali marketplace and a fireworks finale over Toronto City Hall.
  • Admission was free with no tickets or registration required — readers paid only for food and shopping at vendor stalls.
  • The square at 100 Queen Street West is served directly by Queen station on TTC Line 1; listings advised taking transit because downtown parking filled by early evening.

Toronto's flagship Diwali celebration filled Nathan Phillips Square on October 24 and 25, turning the plaza in front of City Hall into two days of music, dance, food and fireworks. The Diwali Festival of Lights, described in event listings as the largest public Diwali event in Toronto and Canada's largest Diwali celebration, ran through the weekend with free admission.

According to the festival listing on CanadaFun, more than 850 artists performed across the weekend. Secret Toronto reported live entertainment and cultural displays on stage throughout each day, with a grand fireworks show capping the night.

What was on at the square

The program paired traditional and contemporary South Asian music and dance with the commercial side of the festival season. Secret Toronto described the city's largest Diwali marketplace at the square, with artisan stalls selling festive decor and jewelry, and food vendors serving Indian street food alongside local festival favourites.

The fireworks finale over City Hall was the headline act both listings pointed readers to. CanadaFun's guide advised arriving before the evening rush, noting the square fills fast on festival nights, and staying for the closing display.

Times, place and getting there

The festival ran at Nathan Phillips Square, 100 Queen Street West, at Queen and Bay in downtown Toronto. Secret Toronto listed hours of 12 p.m. to 10 p.m. on Saturday, October 24 and 12 p.m. to 9 p.m. on Sunday, October 25, while CanadaFun listed programming from noon both days — readers planning around closing fireworks were advised to check the festival's official Instagram page, linked from both listings, for the final schedule.

No advance tickets or registration were required for entry, performances or the fireworks. For transport, Queen station on Line 1 exits directly at the square and Osgoode station is a short walk. Drivers were pointed to the Green P garage under the square at 110 Queen Street West and the Eaton Centre garages, with a warning that downtown event-night parking typically fills by early evening.

Why the location matters

Holding the city's main Diwali celebration at its civic square — rather than in a suburban community hall or a ticketed venue — puts the festival in the same downtown space Toronto uses for its biggest public gatherings. Diwali marks the triumph of light over darkness, and for the Greater Toronto Area's large South Asian population, the Nathan Phillips Square edition has become the public, everyone-welcome version of a festival otherwise centred on homes, temples and neighbourhood events across the region.

CanadaFun's guide also pointed readers to a parallel option north of downtown: the North York Diwali Festival ran October 23-25 at Mel Lastman Square, 5100 Yonge Street, also with free admission — a second civic-square celebration for families in the city's north end.

What it signals

A two-day, 850-performer, fireworks-closed festival on Toronto's main civic square is a measure of how mainstream Diwali has become in Canada's largest city. The event required no community membership and no ticket — the barrier to attendance was simply getting downtown — which is the point of staging a diaspora festival as a city festival, open to neighbours who may know Diwali only as the lights and sweets of late October.
